html:
The Lipan Apache are the easternmost of the Apache peoples, a southern Athabaskan people whose homeland covered much of central and southern Texas and northern Mexico. Their ancestors, like other Apache, came south from the far north before the 1500s.

They hunted bison on foot and, from the late 1600s, on horseback, and farmed small plots by rivers. In the 1700s the Comanche pushed them south. In 1757 the Spanish founded the mission of Santa Cruz de San Sabá for them, but the next year Comanche and allied warriors destroyed it. The Lipan fought and traded in turn with Spain, Mexico and Texas, and were hunted by the Texan and American armies. By the late 1800s the survivors had scattered; some joined the Mescalero in New Mexico. A Lipan Apache tribe is recognised by the state of Texas today.
